Moral Foundations Theory is a framework that separates human morality into the following categories:

  - Care/Harm: related to our long evolution as mammals with attachment systems
    and an ability to feel (and dislike) the pain of others. It underlies the
    virtues of kindness, gentleness, and nurturance.

  - Loyalty/Betrayal: related to our long history as tribal creatures able to
    form shifting coalitions. It is active anytime people feel that it is "one
    for all and all for one." It underlies the virtues of patriotism and
    self-sacrifice for the group.

  - Authority/Subversion: shaped by our long primate history of hierarchical
    social interactions. It underlies virtues of leadership and followership,
    including deference to prestigious authority figures and respect for
    traditions.

  - Sanctity/Purity: shaped by the psychology of disgust and contamination. It
    underlies notions of striving to live in an elevated, less carnal, more
    noble, and more "natural" way (often present in religious narratives). This
    foundation underlies the widespread idea that the body is a temple that can
    be desecrated by immoral activities and contaminants (an idea not unique to
    religious traditions). It underlies the virtues of self-discipline,
    self-improvement, naturalness, and spirituality.

  - Equality: related to our intuitions about equal treatment and equal outcome
    for individuals.

  - Proportionality: related to our intuitions about individuals getting
    rewarded in proportion to their merit or contribution.

New Labour’s 2001 manifesto sets out a second‑term programme to fulfil Britain’s potential by putting power, wealth and opportunity in the hands of the many, not the few. Building on four years of stability and reform, it offers an optimistic, modernising agenda: an active, enabling state working in partnership with people, business and the voluntary sector; investment matched with reform; rights matched by responsibilities. The choice is clear—progress with stability, or a return to Conservative boom and bust, cuts, privatisation and European isolation.

Since 1997, Labour has laid firm foundations: the lowest inflation and unemployment for a generation; over one million more in work; typical mortgages around £1,200 a year lower than under the Tories; the best‑ever primary school results; 17,000 more nurses; crime down 10%; devolution strengthening the UK; constructive leadership in Europe and on international debt relief. Three of five first‑term pledges have been delivered early, all within five years.

Ambitions for a second term focus on five fronts:
- Economic stability and wider prosperity: keep inflation and interest rates low with sound public finances; raise productivity through skills, technology and infrastructure; help seven million adults without basic skills; aim for full employment in every region.
- World‑class public services: sustain investment and empower staff to reform; build on primary gains to transform secondary schools; modernise the NHS to deliver faster treatment, free at the point of use; extend access to culture and sport.
- A modern welfare state: a work‑first benefits system underpinned by rights and responsibilities; stronger support for children and families via tax and benefits; better cash and services for pensioners.
- Strong, safe communities: reform criminal justice to catch, punish and rehabilitate; tackle the causes of crime; empower local communities.
- Britain strong in the world: engage and lead in Europe, support EU enlargement, fight global poverty and climate change; the British people will have the final say on joining the euro.

Ten goals for 2010 include sustained stability, rising living standards, higher secondary standards with expanded higher education, a faster free NHS, full employment region‑wide, opportunity for children and security for pensioners, a modern justice system, accountable local government, British leadership in a reformed EU, and action on global poverty and climate.

Five pledges for the next five years:
1) Low mortgages, low inflation, sound public finances.
2) 10,000 extra teachers and higher secondary standards.
3) 20,000 extra nurses and 10,000 extra doctors in a reformed NHS.
4) 6,000 extra police to record levels.
5) Pensioners’ winter fuel payment retained; minimum wage rising to £4.20.

Head and heart now align: choose stability not boom and bust; investment not cuts; engagement not isolation—opportunity for all hard‑working families, not privileges for a few.

TEXT_G:
Scottish National Party Manifesto 2001 – Summary

We stand for Scotland. Electing SNP MPs is a vote for Independence, for completing the powers of the Scottish Parliament, and for MPs who always put Scotland first. The more SNP MPs, the stronger the mandate for a referendum; a majority would trigger it. Meanwhile, SNP MPs will press immediately for more powers, better deals, and protection from Westminster’s failings.

Independence vision: a just, caring, enterprising Scotland using normal powers every nation has—control of revenues, welfare and investment—to deliver world-class public services. We will harness Scotland’s wealth by creating a sovereign Scottish Fund for Future Generations from oil revenues, and a not-for-profit Scottish Trust for Public Investment to replace costly PFI/PPP and drive infrastructure renewal.

Constitution and democracy: an independent, written constitution with inclusive citizenship; the Queen retained as Head of State subject to referendum; proportional representation at all levels; cut quangos and make remaining ones accountable; strong, opportunity-rich civil service.

Education and young people: abolish tuition fees; rebuild maintenance support; establish an Education Convention; reduce P1–P3 class sizes to 18 in phases; end misleading league tables; refurbish schools via STPI; support McCrone; promote Gaelic medium education; embed anti-racism; improve inclusion and special needs support; votes at 16; strengthen children’s rights with a powerful Commissioner.

Jobs and economy: Scotland-specific strategy—massive infrastructure, broadband everywhere, and national reskilling; streamline enterprise agencies; market Scotland globally; overhaul tourism into a marketing-led, access-focused industry.

Fair work: devolve and improve the New Deal; raise the minimum wage to £4.36 for all ages, with small business support; guarantee union rights and back EU worker protections.

Environment and utilities: make Scotland a sustainability leader; oppose the UK climate levy’s damage to hydro; deliver a State of the Nation Environmental Audit and a National Environment Plan; 12% of energy and 25% of electricity from renewables by 2010; no new nuclear, lead in decommissioning; embed polluter pays and resource efficiency; reform water charges and governance, stop backdoor privatisation.

Health and care: take politics out of the NHS with a National Health Care Commission; end postcode treatment—HTBS rulings binding; free fruit in schools and healthier meals; free dental check-ups; freeze and review prescription charges; invest via STPI in equipment, cleaner hospitals, 1,500 more nurses, and halve waits; free personal care for all elderly people.

Europe and the world: Scotland in Europe—pro-subsidiarity, anti-superstate; euro only by consent when conditions fit; independence brings full EU representation. Remove Trident; oppose US missile defence; negotiate phased withdrawal from NATO’s nuclear structures; create a professional Scottish Defence Force; ethical defence exports. Build business-focused external offices; meet UN aid targets; cancel debt; untie aid.

Culture, sport and language: devolve broadcasting, secure a Scottish Six; focus sport on communities; reform arts funding, create a national theatre and Scottish Lottery; secure status for Gaelic and promote Scots.

Social justice, housing and equality: a national anti-poverty strategy; end asylum vouchers; transfer housing debt, invest without wholesale stock transfer; core fund the voluntary sector; tackle homelessness; strengthen equality and disability rights; tougher on drug dealers with Drug Courts.

Safety and justice: 1,000 more police; empower courts against youth offending with parental compensation orders; lifelong restrictions for high-risk sex offenders; speed cases; retain Scottish justice receipts in Scotland.

Tax, local government and rural Scotland: honest, transparent tax—comprehensive review with no overall rise without mandate; immediately cut fuel duty by 10p/gal funded by a new 5p band on income over £100k; review local government finance including local income tax; PR/STV for councils. Support rural services, cut fuel burdens, improve transport and digital access.

Agriculture, fisheries, land: post–foot-and-mouth strategy; fair EU playing field; compensated tie-ups and technical conservation; reform CFP with zonal councils; salmon farming inquiry; empower community buy-outs; national freshwater policy.

Pensions and social security: restore the earnings link, spread winter payments weekly; streamline benefit delivery, boost take-up; fairer disability and carers’ support; fix WFTC traps.

Transport: secure Scotland’s fair UK share; invest via STPI; regional transport authorities; public share in Railtrack; reopen and electrify priority lines; concessionary travel; targeted road upgrades; lower ferry fares and abolish Skye Bridge tolls; expand direct flights and cut airport costs.
